title: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every regular language there is a pumping length p such that any word of length at least p splits as xyz with |xy| at most p, |y| positive, and xyⁱz in the language for every nonnegative i.
latex: |w| ≥ p ⇒ w = xyz and xyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0
short: Long words in a regular language contain a loop that can be repeated arbitrarily.
long: Long words in a regular language contain a loop that can be repeated arbitrarily. It is a standard tool for proving that a language is not regular, though satisfying the lemma does not prove regularity.
proof: A DFA with p states repeats a state while reading the first p+1 symbols; the loop between repeats can be pumped.
consequence: It gives elementary separations such as the nonregularity of equal numbers of a's and b's.

title: Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: For every context-free language there is a pumping length p such that any long enough word splits as uvxyz with |vxy| at most p, |vy| positive, and uvⁱxyⁱz in the language for every nonnegative i.
latex: w = uvxyz, uvⁱxyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0
short: Repeated nonterminals in a parse tree create two synchronized pumpable substrings.
long: Repeated nonterminals in a parse tree create two synchronized pumpable substrings. The two pumped pieces are what distinguish it from the regular pumping lemma, and the length bound on vxy constrains their positions.
proof: In a parse tree of sufficient height, a path repeats a nonterminal; replace the smaller subtree by the larger one repeatedly.
consequence: It proves, for example, that the language of strings with three equal blocks is not context-free.

title: Myhill–Nerode Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: A language is regular if and only if the number of equivalence classes of the relation of having the same set of acceptable continuations is finite.
latex: L regular iff the residual equivalence has finite index
short: Regular languages are exactly those with only finitely many distinguishable states.
long: Regular languages are exactly those with only finitely many distinguishable states. The equivalence classes become the states of the minimal DFA.
proof: Define x ~ y if for all z, xz in L iff yz in L; finite index gives a DFA whose states are classes, and a DFA gives finitely many classes.
consequence: It both characterizes regularity and gives an algorithm for minimal automata.

title: Undecidability of Context-Free Language Equivalence
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: No algorithm decides whether two context-free grammars generate the same language.
short: Even restricted grammars hide the halting problem.
long: Even restricted grammars hide the halting problem. Emptiness and finiteness of context-free languages are decidable, but equivalence and disjointness are not.
proof: Reduce the Post correspondence problem by building a grammar whose universality holds exactly when a PCP solution exists.
consequence: It marks the decidability boundary just above regular languages.

title: Undecidable Emptiness for Context-Sensitive Grammars
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Deciding whether a context-sensitive grammar generates at least one terminal string is undecidable.
short: A grammar with length-bounded rewriting can still encode halting.
long: A grammar with length-bounded rewriting can still encode halting. Context-sensitive languages correspond to nondeterministic linear bounded automata, whose acceptance problem is undecidable despite bounded space.
proof: Encode a Turing machine computation as a derivation of an accepting history, which exists only if the machine halts.
consequence: It shows that undecidability can occur even when every derivation is length-bounded.

title: Recursively Enumerable Languages Are Not Closed Under Complement
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The complement of a recursively enumerable language need not be recursively enumerable; the complement of the halting set is the standard counterexample.
latex: RE is not closed under complement
short: A recognizer for yes instances does not yield a recognizer for no instances.
long: A recognizer for yes instances does not yield a recognizer for no instances. Closure under union and intersection holds; complement is exactly the operation that turns semi-decidability into decidability when both sides are available.
proof: If both a set and its complement were enumerable, dovetailing their recognizers would decide the set, contradicting halting undecidability.
consequence: The asymmetry explains why positive and negative evidence differ in computation.

title: Decidable Syntactic Properties Do Not Violate Rice's Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Rice's theorem concerns semantic properties of the accepted language; purely syntactic properties such as containing a given instruction are decidable by scanning the program text.
short: The scope of Rice's theorem is language-level properties, not source-code features.
long: The scope of Rice's theorem is language-level properties, not source-code features. Program equivalence and totality are semantic and hence undecidable, while counting characters in the source is trivially decidable.
proof: A finite scan of a finite program decides any fixed syntactic question, so the property is not language-invariant and Rice's theorem does not apply.
consequence: It clarifies which static analyses can be complete and which must be conservative.

title: The Universal Turing Machine
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: There exists a single Turing machine that, given an encoding of any machine M and input w, simulates M on w.
short: One machine can run every machine when handed its description.
long: One machine can run every machine when handed its description. The encoding includes transition tables and tape contents; the universal machine loops by decoding and executing one simulated step at a time.
proof: Encode configurations as strings and implement the transition function of the simulated machine by string manipulation.
consequence: It is the theoretical foundation of stored-program computers and interpreters.

title: Partial Recursive Functions Equal Turing Computable Functions
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The partial functions computable by Turing machines are exactly the μ-recursive functions generated by constants, successor, projections, composition, primitive recursion, and unbounded minimization.
short: Several seemingly different definitions of effective computation coincide.
long: Several seemingly different definitions of effective computation coincide. This equivalence is one formulation of the Church–Turing thesis in its provable part.
proof: Implement recursion and minimization with Turing machine loops, and conversely code configurations numerically to simulate machines by μ-recursion.
consequence: It justifies choosing whichever formal model is most convenient.

title: The Ackermann Function Is Not Primitive Recursive
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The Ackermann function is total and computable but grows faster than every primitive recursive function.
latex: A(m,n) eventually dominates every primitive recursive f
short: Unbounded recursion produces growth beyond the primitive recursive fragment.
long: Unbounded recursion produces growth beyond the primitive recursive fragment. Fixed slices A(m,·) form a hierarchy: each is primitive recursive, but the diagonal function escapes the whole hierarchy.
proof: Show by induction on m that A(m,·) dominates increasingly high levels, and every primitive recursive function is eventually dominated by some level.
consequence: It separates primitive recursion from general recursion.

title: Decidable Equivalence of Regular Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Emptiness, containment, and equivalence of regular languages are all decidable.
short: Finite automata support complete algorithms for their basic decision problems.
long: Finite automata support complete algorithms for their basic decision problems. Build an automaton for the symmetric difference and check whether any accepting state is reachable from the start state.
proof: Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so the symmetric difference is regular; reachability in a finite graph is decidable.
consequence: It contrasts with the undecidability of the same questions for context-free languages.

title: Quines and the Recursion Theorem
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Self-reproducing programs exist because the recursion theorem lets a program compute its own source description.
short: Self-reference is a theorem, not a programming accident.
long: Self-reference is a theorem, not a programming accident. A quine prints its own code using two copies of a template, one as data and one as instructions; the recursion theorem explains why this is always possible.
proof: Apply the recursion theorem to the computable function that, given an index, produces a program printing that index.
consequence: It connects computability theory with real self-referential software.

title: Oracle Separations for P versus NP
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: There is an oracle A with Pᴬ = NPᴬ and an oracle B with Pᴮ ≠ NPᴮ.
short: Relative to different oracles, the P versus NP question has different answers.
long: Relative to different oracles, the P versus NP question has different answers. Baker, Gill, and Solovay constructed oracles both making the classes collapse and making them separate.
proof: A collapsing oracle is built closed under efficient self-reduction; a separating oracle diagonalizes against all polynomial-time machines.
consequence: Any proof of P versus NP must use non-relativizing techniques.

title: Turing Degrees and the Halting Degree
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Turing degrees are equivalence classes of sets mutually computable from one another, ordered by reducibility, with computable sets forming the least degree zero and the halting set forming 0′.
short: Degrees measure how much noncomputability a set contains.
long: Degrees measure how much noncomputability a set contains. The structure of degrees is rich: there are incomparable degrees and infinitely many degrees between zero and zero prime.
proof: Mutual reducibility is an equivalence relation; the jump of any set is strictly above it, giving 0 <ₜ 0′.
consequence: It provides the standard taxonomy of unsolvability.

title: Undecidability of Finiteness for Turing Machine Languages
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: No algorithm decides whether a Turing machine accepts only finitely many strings.
short: Even the question of whether a recognizer accepts finitely much is undecidable.
long: Even the question of whether a recognizer accepts finitely much is undecidable. Finiteness is a nontrivial semantic index set, so Rice's theorem applies directly.
proof: If finiteness were decidable, one could decide halting by constructing a machine that accepts all strings unless a simulated machine halts, in which case it accepts only finitely many.
consequence: It illustrates the reach of Rice's theorem beyond emptiness.

title: Undecidable Emptiness for Turing Machines
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Deciding whether a Turing machine accepts no input at all is undecidable.
short: We cannot decide in general whether a program accepts anything.
long: We cannot decide in general whether a program accepts anything. This is the semantic property of emptiness, one of the simplest nontrivial properties covered by Rice's theorem.
proof: Emptiness depends only on the accepted language and is true for some machines and false for others, so Rice's theorem gives undecidability.
consequence: It is a common reduction source for other undecidability results.

title: Bounded Halting Is Decidable
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: Given a machine, input, and explicit time bound t, deciding whether the machine halts within t steps is decidable by direct simulation.
short: Undecidability comes from unbounded time, not from simulating finite runs.
long: Undecidability comes from unbounded time, not from simulating finite runs. The simulation costs at most t steps and can be implemented on a universal machine.
proof: Simulate the machine for at most t steps and answer yes exactly when a halting configuration is reached.
consequence: It explains why bounded model checking is feasible while general verification is not.

title: From Halting Undecidability to Incompleteness
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The undecidability of the halting problem implies that no sound, effectively axiomatized theory can prove all true statements of arithmetic.
latex: True arithmetic is not recursively enumerable
short: Incompleteness is the logical shadow of the halting problem.
long: Incompleteness is the logical shadow of the halting problem. If a complete sound effective theory of arithmetic existed, one could decide halting by searching for proofs of the corresponding arithmetic statements.
proof: Encode halting as an arithmetic sentence; a decision procedure for theoremhood would decide halting, contradicting undecidability.
consequence: Computability and proof theory express the same fundamental limitation.

title: Trakhtenbrot's Theorem on Finite Satisfiability
subject: Computability & Logic
statement: The set of first-order sentences that have a finite model is undecidable.
short: Restricting attention to finite structures destroys the decidability of satisfiability.
long: Restricting attention to finite structures destroys the decidability of satisfiability. By contrast, validity over all structures is semi-decidable by completeness, and validity over finite structures is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable.
proof: Trakhtenbrot reduced the halting problem to the existence of a finite model whose relations encode a halting computation.
consequence: It separates finite model theory from classical model theory.

title: The Complexity Class P
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: P is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time bounded by a polynomial in the input length.
short: Polynomial time is the standard formalization of efficient computation.
long: Polynomial time is the standard formalization of efficient computation. The class is robust across reasonable machine models because simulations cost only polynomial overhead.
proof: Definition; closure under composition of polynomial bounds shows model independence.
consequence: P anchors the main classification of tractable problems.

title: The Complexity Class NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NP is the class of decision problems whose yes instances have polynomial-size certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently problems solved by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine.
short: A solution is easy to check even when finding it may be hard.
long: A solution is easy to check even when finding it may be hard. The verifier definition avoids reliance on nondeterministic hardware and is the one used in practice.
proof: Guess a certificate nondeterministically and run the deterministic verifier; conversely, record the nondeterministic choices as the certificate.
consequence: It captures a huge family of natural search and optimization problems.

title: co-NP and Its Relation to NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: co-NP is the class of complements of NP languages; it contains problems whose no instances have short certificates.
latex: coNP = { complement of L : L ∈ NP }
short: NP certifies yes answers; co-NP certifies no answers.
long: NP certifies yes answers; co-NP certifies no answers. TAUTOLOGY is in co-NP because a falsifying assignment is a short certificate for a no instance.
proof: Complement the accepting and rejecting states of a nondeterministic polynomial-time verifier.
consequence: NP = co-NP is widely disbelieved and would imply surprising collapses.

title: P Equals NP Implies NP Equals co-NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If P equals NP then NP equals co-NP, since deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement.
short: Deterministic algorithms give yes and no answers symmetrically.
long: Deterministic algorithms give yes and no answers symmetrically. The contrapositive says NP differing from co-NP would settle P versus NP.
proof: A deterministic polynomial-time machine can flip its accept and reject states, so P = coP; substituting P = NP gives NP = coNP.
consequence: It is the simplest consequence of a collapse of P and NP.

title: NP-Complete Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: A language is NP-complete if it belongs to NP and every language in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
latex: L ∈ NPC iff L ∈ NP and ∀ A ∈ NP : A ≤ₚ L
short: One efficient algorithm for an NP-complete problem would solve all of NP.
long: One efficient algorithm for an NP-complete problem would solve all of NP. Completeness is defined relative to a reduction notion; the standard one is polynomial-time many-one reducibility.
proof: SAT is NP-complete by Cook–Levin, and transitivity of polynomial reductions transfers completeness to any NP problem SAT reduces to.
consequence: It provides a rigorous notion of the hardest problems in NP.

title: co-NP-Complete Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: A problem is co-NP-complete if it lies in co-NP and every co-NP problem polynomial-time reduces to it; TAUTOLOGY and UNSAT are standard examples.
short: The hardest no-certificate problems mirror NP-complete ones.
long: The hardest no-certificate problems mirror NP-complete ones. A problem is co-NP-complete exactly when its complement is NP-complete.
proof: Complement a polynomial reduction to SAT to obtain a reduction to UNSAT or TAUTOLOGY.
consequence: It clarifies which problems would collapse NP and co-NP if shown NP-complete.
